title: The Elements
tagline: Thirteen books that defined the shape of reason forever.

scenes.text: Alexandria, 300 BCE. The greatest library the world has ever seen. Euclid of Alexandria is writing — not just recording what he knows, but building a logical architecture that will hold for two thousand years: thirteen books proving everything in geometry from five simple assumptions.

scenes.speaker: Euclid
scenes.text: A point has no part. A line has breadth-less length. Begin there. Everything else follows.

challenge.question: Euclid worked in which great ancient city?
challenge.fact: Euclid worked at the Library of Alexandria under Ptolemy I around 300 BCE. When Ptolemy asked if there was a shorter way to learn geometry, Euclid reportedly replied: 'There is no royal road to geometry.'

scenes.text: Euclid's proof that prime numbers are infinite is one of the first genuine proofs in mathematics — a demonstration so elegant it appears unchanged in textbooks today. His method: assume finitely many primes, multiply them together and add one, then show the contradiction.

scenes.speaker: King Ptolemy
scenes.text: Euclid. Is there not a shortcut to geometry?

scenes.speaker: Euclid
scenes.text: There is no royal road to geometry.

challenge.instruction: Ptolemy wants a shortcut, a student wants a profit, a sceptic wants a picture. Answer each of them as Euclid did — with proof.
challenge.fact: Euclid's Elements (c. 300 BCE) comprises 13 books and 465 propositions. It was used in university geometry courses until the early 20th century — over 2,000 years of continuous use.

challenge.instruction: The Elements begins with definitions and builds every proof on them. Fill the crossword with the words Euclid's geometry starts from.
challenge.fact: Euclid's proof of the Pythagorean theorem occupies a full page of the Elements and uses nothing but logic. It remains one of the most beautiful proofs in all of mathematics.

scenes.text: Eratosthenes, who would later calculate the circumference of the Earth with remarkable accuracy, studied in the same tradition as Euclid. Each generation of Alexandrian scholars built on the previous — standing, as Newton would say two thousand years later, on the shoulders of giants.

challenge.instruction: Eratosthenes, librarian at Alexandria, turned Euclid's geometry on the Earth itself. Read the gnomon's noon shadow and measure the planet.
challenge.fact: Eratosthenes' method rests on a theorem of the Elements: a straight line falling on two parallel lines makes the alternate angles equal (Book I, Proposition 29). The sun's rays at Syene and Alexandria are the parallels.

params.title: The Scrolls of the Mouseion
params.intro: New scrolls have come to Alexandria and the catalogue slips are mixed. Match each Greek author with the work the scholars of the Mouseion copied and studied.
params.fact: Under Ptolemy I and II the Mouseion of Alexandria gathered scholars and books from the whole Greek world. Callimachus later catalogued the Library in his Pinakes, 120 books of lists of authors and their works.

challenge.instruction: The scholars who came after Euclid built on the Library's books. Match each author to the scroll Alexandria kept — before the slips shift again.
challenge.fact: Euclid's Elements was copied and commented on at Alexandria for centuries. Theon of Alexandria's edition of the 4th century CE is the source of almost every manuscript that survives.

scenes.speaker: Euclid
scenes.text: Anaxagoras and Aspasia hold Carthage together, and a follower stands with them. One card alone will not move them. Bring Chanakya with me, add both followers, and strike twice.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 2 · Strength in Numbers. Over two turns stack Euclid, Chanakya and both followers at Carthage, then win two attacks against the rival side.
challenge.fact: An attack compares whole sides at a location, not single cards. Two Great People and two followers in the same stat outweigh a rival who arrived first, and each win sends one rival card back to its owner's hand.
